Baby & Child

Teaching everyday skills to children, one step at a time

Updated: November 14, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

“Put your things away” sounds like one instruction. For a child holding a jacket, it might mean finding a hook, locating the loop inside the collar, turning the jacket and lifting it high enough to hang. If the hook is out of reach, repeating the instruction will not help. Watch one attempt together. The point where your child stops often tells you which part to teach or change first.

Choose a task your child wants to use

Start with something that matters to your child today, such as putting a favorite book into a bag or getting a jacket off without help. Ask what they would like to try. A child might choose between two activities by speaking, pointing, signing or handing you an object. Even if the larger routine is necessary, there can still be a choice about which part to practice and when to try it.

Set up both the object and the child for success. A chair that lets their feet rest securely, a larger handle or a quieter corner may make a hard action possible. Let them show you how much they can already do before offering help. A child who pushes a plate away when asked to set the table might be unsure where it goes, worried about dropping it, tired or simply finished with the activity.

Give one cue your child can act on

Get close enough to be heard and put the object where your child can comfortably find it. If the television is competing for attention, turn it down. Say exactly what the next action is in familiar words. “Put the napkin beside your plate” is easier to act on than “Get everything ready.” A calm voice, a pointing gesture or a familiar sign may carry the message more clearly than extra explanation.

Give the child time to respond. Attention might look like reaching towards the object, turning an ear to your voice or watching your hands. Looking into your eyes is unnecessary. If several reminders produce no movement, ask whether your child wants to see you do it. Repeating the same words more loudly can leave the original difficulty in place.

Show the movement, then hand over the turn

Use your own materials when possible so the child can watch and keep hold of theirs. To show how a zipper opens, hold your own bag steady with one hand, slowly draw the tab with the other, then let go. Say “Hold here” at the moment you steady the bag. Try the movement from beside the child if the view from across the table makes the directions look reversed.

Demonstration works for communication too. You might pause at the door and wave to someone arriving, or point to “more” on a communication board as you ask for another turn in a game. Leave room for the child to greet someone, request a turn or say “finished” in their own way. Smiling on cue, copying your voice or repeating a particular sentence need not be part of learning what a greeting or request does.

Find the small actions inside the job

Do the activity yourself once, looking for points where your hands change jobs. Packing a picture book for a visit might mean opening the bag, holding the opening wide, sliding the book inside and closing the top. If “open the bag” still feels too large, break that part down again. One hand steadies the bag while the other finds the pull and draws it to the corner.

Try a simple visual sequence for a child who finds spoken instructions hard to retain. Take photos of your own bag open, the book inside and the closed bag, or draw the three states. Put the pictures where the child can consult them. Check together that the pictures make sense. If an abstract symbol is confusing, the real item or a demonstration can be easier to understand. A child may continue to use the pictures independently for as long as they are useful.

Start at the beginning or let the child finish

With forward chaining, the child learns the first action, and the adult helps with the rest. For the book bag, the child might learn to open the top while you hold the opening, pack the book and close the bag. Once opening is comfortable, give them the next action as well. Choose this approach if recognizing how to get started is the useful part right now.

With backward chaining, you complete the early actions and the child takes the last turn. The order of the task itself stays the same. Put the book inside, bring the top of the bag together and offer the zipper pull to close it. On a later attempt the child can put the book in and close the bag. Taking on the step just before a familiar finish can make the point of the new action easier to see.

Try a dressing routine without the morning rush

Choose a garment your child likes and a time when nobody is hurrying to get out. For example, start with an open cardigan and a seated child who wants to put it on. Lay it out in a familiar position, find the first sleeve, guide one arm through, find the second sleeve and settle the fabric across the shoulders. Your child might prefer a different sequence. Try it their way if it is comfortable and works.

If the last action is reachable, help with the earlier steps as agreed, then let the child smooth the fabric into place. Once this feels familiar, offer the second sleeve and let them complete both actions. If reaching behind is difficult or the fabric scratches, address that first. Removing a tag, turning the garment around on a table, choosing a softer layer or practicing with a different fastening can change what is possible more than repeated instructions.

Gradually reduce prompts and keep useful supports

A prompt is a cue that helps the next action happen. Begin with what your child needs. You might show the movement on your own bag, use a short phrase, point to the tab, or simply leave the bag where they expect it. On another try, pause before giving a familiar reminder and see whether the child starts. If they get stuck, offer the hint that helped last time. Removing every reminder at once can turn a familiar task into a guessing game.

Ask before providing physical help. “Would you like me to hold the bag?” leaves the child in charge of their own hands. If they ask for help moving an object or clothing, agree what you are going to do and stop when they pull away or signal a break. Keep their communication aid within reach. A larger zipper pull, a stable chair or a picture guide may be part of the child's own method even after your spoken prompts have faded.

Make practice easy to repeat

A short turn within an ordinary routine gives the child a real reason to try. A second chance when putting a book away after the visit may be more welcome than emptying the bag ten times at the front door. A child who can put on a cardigan after lunch may need help when they are cold, tired or already waiting for the school bus. Help with the immediate need and return to teaching at a better time.

Make feedback specific. “You kept the bag still while you moved the zip” tells the child what worked. If it jammed, try “A corner of the book is in the way. Shall we move it?” before asking for another attempt. Let the child tell you how much praise or attention they want. Give one useful suggestion, and stop the practice if their hands hurt or they become upset.

When the same step stays difficult

Watch whether the difficulty is remembering the sequence, seeing or hearing the cue, gripping an object, coordinating two hands, or tolerating a sensation. A child who opens the bag easily when someone else holds it has shown you something quite specific. You can steady it against a surface and see whether that frees the other hand. A child who can perform each action separately may benefit from laying the objects out in order.

If a child consistently struggles with familiar daily activities, experiences pain or loses a skill they used before, discuss what you have noticed with their clinician. An occupational therapist can look at practical tasks and equipment. A speech and language professional can help find a communication method that fits. Bring one concrete example of the step, the help you offered and what happened. You can ask for developmental assessment whenever you have a concern.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Match the size of each step and the way you demonstrate it to your child's movement, communication and sensory needs.

Give the child control over physical help and gradually make room for them to start the next action.

Seek professional guidance for pain, a skill that has been lost or continuing concerns about practical tasks.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record a useful step, the cue your child prefers and questions for an appointment. An occupational therapist or clinician can observe the task directly when progress or comfort is a concern.

When to seek help

Choose age-appropriate safe materials and provide the supervision the task needs. Stop if the child signals discomfort or asks for a break. Pain, loss of a familiar skill or persistent difficulties with everyday activities deserve assessment.

Evidence notes updated: November 14, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Pick a useful task and watch the point where your child needs help.
  • Use a short cue, a slow demonstration or a visual sequence the child can consult.
  • Teach the first step and add the next, or let the child complete the last step and work back from there.
  • Pause before giving a familiar prompt and keep an aid or adaptation that helps the child participate.
  • Respect a request to stop and seek advice for pain, loss of a skill or persistent difficulty with daily tasks.

Frequently asked questions

Why teach a child the small steps of an everyday activity?

Breaking a routine into actions shows the child what to try next and helps you see where the difficulty lies. The child can take a real turn even if an adult still handles some parts. Choosing a task they want to use gives the practice a purpose.

What are three ways to teach a new skill?

Give a short instruction, show the movement or teach the task as a sequence of small actions. You can combine them. For instance, point to a zip, slowly open your own bag and then offer the child a turn with theirs.

What makes an instruction easier to follow?

Get the child's attention in a comfortable way, reduce distractions and use familiar words for one action at a time. Point, sign or show the object if that helps. Pause so the child can process the cue and communicate whether they want help.

How can I help a child remember what comes next?

Place a few photos or drawings of the actual task near the place it happens. Demonstrate how to check the next picture, then leave time for the child to use it. Use an object or a spoken cue instead if that is more accessible.

How do I decide whether to teach forward or backward?

If the child is interested in getting started, let them take the first step while you finish. If reaching the result is motivating and the final action is manageable, prepare the earlier steps and let them finish. You can change the approach if the chosen step proves difficult.

What if my child looks away or refuses a turn?

Looking away alone does not tell you whether the child is listening. They may attend to the object, need extra time, be overwhelmed or want to stop. Offer a pause or a simpler option and accept their response. A refusal is a reason to look at the task and circumstances.

Should I hold my child's hands to make the movement?

Offer a demonstration or stabilize the object first. Check that your child welcomes any hands-on assistance and stop if they pull away or ask you to stop. A child can learn while using an adapted tool or asking another person to help with one part.
